newsitem.title: VATICAN: Pope, Carey, stress commitment to unity.
newsitem.headline: Pope, Carey, stress commitment to unity.

text.p: Pope John Paul and the Archbishop of Canterbury George Carey reaffirmed the commitment of their Roman Catholic and Anglican churches on Tuesday to strive for unity despite formidable obstacles.
The 76-year-old Pope welcomed Carey to the Vatican at the start of the Anglican leader's first official visit to the centre of Roman Catholicism.
"Our churches bear the marks of separation and division," Carey told the Pope.
"We cannot undo overnight doctrinal differences and the bitternesses that have resulted from the legacy of history but we are able to confront them as fellow Christians...."
The two churches, which split in 1534 when King Henry VIII broke with Rome over papal authority, are still divided over the question and more recently hit a stumbling block over women priests.
Carey, who will hold full talks with the Pope on Thursday, spoke of the "absolute commitment...to the full visible unity of God's Church" that he and the Anglican church supported.
The Polish Pope spoke of the drive for unity, saying that despite differences, Anglicans and Catholics had not ceased to be brothers and sisters in God.
"The task before us is to strengthen that bond, until we reach the full unity that is Christ's will for us," he said.

Carey became spiritual leader of the 70 million member worldwide Anglican communion in 1990. Two years later the Church of England, mother church of Anglicanism, voted to allow women priests in a move that severely tested relations between Canterbury and Rome. The first were ordained in 1994.
Carey underscored the progress that had been made in 30 years of theological dialogue between Anglicans and Catholics.
Neither the Pope nor Carey specifically mentioned obstacles to unity, among which women priests is the most formidable.

In 1995 the Vatican said the Catholic ban on female ordination was a definitive, infallible and unquestionable part of Church doctrine. The ruling would make it difficult if not impossible for a future Pope to change the ruling for some time.

The Catholic Church says it does not have the authority to allow women to become priests because Christ, in a free and sovereign way, chose only men as his apostles and was therefore reflecting "divine will".
A handful of Anglican bishops, more than 300 clergy and thousands of lay members have converted to Catholicism because of their opposition to women priests.
Papal primacy -- recognition of the Pope's supreme authority over any unified Christian church -- has been another thorny issues facing theologians in ecumenical dialogue.

In a move with potentially historic consequences, the Pope said in a 1995 encyclical that for the sake of unity he was willing to seek an accommodation with other Christian denominations on the future role of the papacy.
But he made clear he would not accept a symbolic papacy without teeth and that Rome would have to hold the primary place among Christians because St Peter, the first Pope, died there.
